Reading list, mostly from Hodges Figgis on Dawson Street and the second-hand shelf in Books Upstairs.

- [x] Camus, *The Myth of Sisyphus* (Penguin Modern Classics, trans. Justin O'Brien). Finished 4 Aug 2024. "One must imagine Sisyphus happy", p. 123. Read on the Enterprise train to Belfast and back.
- [x] Sartre, *Existentialism Is a Humanism*. The lecture of 29 Oct 1945 at the Club Maintenant, packed to fainting. One sitting, 70 pages.
- [ ] Sartre, *Being and Nothingness* (Barnes trans.). Two attempts. Stuck both times at p. 86, just after the café waiter and bad faith. Third attempt planned for the summer.
- [x] Beauvoir, *The Ethics of Ambiguity*. Jan 2025. Better than Sartre at saying what follows for how to live.
- [ ] Kierkegaard, *Fear and Trembling*. Bought 11 Jan 2025, €12.99. Lost the book club vote to Bakewell 3 to 2.
- [x] Sarah Bakewell, *At the Existentialist Café* (2016). Second read. The apricot cocktails at the Bec-de-Gaz on rue du Montparnasse, 1933, where Aron tells Sartre about phenomenology.
- [ ] Dostoevsky, *Notes from Underground*. On the bedside table since October.
- [x] Camus, *The Plague*. Re-read in 2020, of course.
- [ ] Heidegger, *Being and Time*. Honestly, no. Maybe the Inwood introduction instead.
- [ ] Simone Weil, *Gravity and Grace*. Not an existentialist, recommended by Inés from book club anyway.

Thoughts so far:
- Camus is the one I'd give a seventeen-year-old.
- Bad faith is the most useful idea for a teacher. "I'm only doing what the curriculum says" is bad faith, most days.
